509e71dde3fb_e96db098f388: This section, the introduction of the paper, focuses on the development and application of biocompatible hydrogels, particularly those composed of silk fibroin (SF) and hyaluronic acid (HA), in the biomedical field. It highlights the advantages of these materials, including their biodegradability, biocompatibility, and ability to mimic the extracellular matrix (ECM). The section discusses the limitations of HA alone, leading to the exploration of SF/HA composite hydrogels for improved mechanical properties and bioactivity. It also introduces curcumin as a therapeutic agent with anti-inflammatory and other beneficial properties, motivating the study of curcumin-loaded SF/HA hydrogels. The section sets the stage for the paper's investigation into a simple sonication method for preparing these hydrogels, their characterization using techniques like FTIR, XRD, TGA, and FESEM, and the evaluation of their biological activity through cell viability assays.
509e71dde3fb_82a0cd486663: This section details the specific materials used in the study, focusing on the preparation and sourcing of key components for hydrogel synthesis. It begins by describing the rearing of *Bombyx mori* silk cocoons and the subsequent extraction of silk fibroin (SF) through a process involving shredding, boiling in 0.1 M Na₂CO₃ for 120 minutes, rinsing, and drying for 24 hours. Hyaluronic acid sodium (MW 8 x 10⁵ Da, >90% purity) was obtained from Monteloeder, and curcumin (99% purity) was purchased from ChromaDex. Purified water (18.2 MΩ-cm at 25 °C) from a Millipore system was used throughout the experiments. All other chemicals and solvents were of analytical grade and used as received. This section is crucial for reproducibility, outlining the origin and preparation of the essential building blocks for the hydrogels characterized later in the paper.
509e71dde3fb_b9c64fb46f23: This section details the protocol for dissolving silk fibroin (SF) to prepare it for hydrogel synthesis. The process involves dissolving SF in a 9.3 M lithium bromide (LiBr) solution, a common solvent for SF, to create a 20 wt.% SF solution. The dissolution is carried out at 60 °C with stirring for 6 hours, resulting in a yellowish solution. To remove the LiBr salt, the solution undergoes dialysis using a 12 kDa dialysis bag against distilled water for 72 hours, with water changes every 3 hours until a conductivity of less than 2 uS/cm is achieved. Finally, the solution is centrifuged to remove any SF precipitates and concentrated to obtain SF solutions at concentrations of 5 mg/mL and 10 mg/mL, which are then stored at 4 °C. This SF dissolution step is crucial for creating the SF/HA hydrogels described later in the paper.
509e71dde3fb_ffe9d9265cba: This section details the preparation of curcumin-loaded silk fibroin (SF) hydrogels, a crucial step in creating biomaterials for biomedical applications. The process involves dissolving 25 mg of curcumin in 5 mL of 0.1 N NaOH, followed by dilutions to achieve curcumin concentrations of 0.66, 1.25, and 2.5 mg/mL. A fixed volume of 0.5 mL of 10 mg/mL SF solution is then mixed with 0.5 mL of the diluted curcumin solutions, resulting in SF/curcumin mass ratios of 16/1, 8/1, 4/1, and 2/1. The mixtures are sonicated for 20 seconds at 30% amplitude in Eppendorf tubes to induce sol-gel transition, forming the hydrogels, which are subsequently lyophilized. A blank sample without curcumin is also prepared as a control. This section is part of the "Materials and Methods" and provides the methodology for creating one of the key materials characterized and tested for biomedical applications later in the paper.
509e71dde3fb_3c05526fdd5a: This section details the preparation of curcumin-loaded silk fibroin/hyaluronic acid (SF/HA) hydrogels, a crucial step in creating biomaterials for biomedical applications. The process involves creating curcumin solutions in 1 N NaOH at concentrations of 1.25, 2.5, and 5 mg/mL. These solutions are then mixed in equal volumes (0.5 mL) with 10 mg/mL SF/HA solutions (ratios of 80/20, 50/50, and 40/60) to achieve final SF/HA to curcumin mass ratios of 8/1, 4/1, and 2/1. The mixtures are sonicated for 20 seconds at 30% amplitude in Eppendorf tubes to induce sol-gel transition, forming the hydrogels, which are subsequently lyophilized. Table 1, referenced in this section, provides a comprehensive overview of the composition and nomenclature of all prepared samples. This section is essential for understanding the methodology used to create the hydrogels that are later characterized and tested for their biological activity.
509e71dde3fb_ea7c5be6ac38: This section provides a detailed compositional breakdown of the silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), and curcumin hydrogels prepared in the study. It outlines the mass ratios of SF/HA and SF/curcumin used to create different hydrogel grades, with specific percentages of each component (SF, HA, and curcumin) listed for each sample code (A1-C9). The table serves as a reference for understanding the composition of the hydrogels characterized by techniques such as FTIR, XRD, TGA, and FESEM, and tested for cell viability. The hydrogels were prepared using a sonication method, and the table details the varying weight percentages of each component in the hydrogels. This compositional information is crucial for interpreting the physical, morphological, and biological properties of the hydrogels, and for determining the optimal formulation for biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_8e93a611d611: This section outlines the experimental procedures for characterizing the synthesized hydrogels, focusing on swelling properties, curcumin release kinetics, and structural analysis. It details the swelling test, where dried hydrogels are submerged in deionized water at 25 °C for 24 hours to determine swelling ratio and water uptake. The kinetic release of curcumin is assessed using a self-made USP type 4 flow-through cell apparatus with PBS (pH 7, 0.5% Tween 80) at 37 °C, measuring absorbance at 421 nm every 30 seconds using a UV-Vis spectrometer. Structural characterization involves Attenuated Total Reflectance Fourier Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (ATR-FTIR), using an iS5-Nicolet spectrometer with a Deuterated Triglycine Sulfate detector, averaging 64 scans at a data collection rate of 0.47 scans per second. This section is crucial for understanding the hydrogels' behavior in aqueous environments, their drug release capabilities, and their chemical composition, all vital for assessing their potential biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_d693366cd9ef: This section details the X-ray Diffraction (XRD) methodology employed to characterize the crystalline structure of silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), curcumin, and their composite hydrogels. The XRD analysis was conducted using a D8 Advance diffractometer with CuKα radiation at 40 kV and 30 mA, scanning samples disaggregated in an agate mortar from 5 to 45° at 0.05° intervals with a rotation speed of 30 rpm. The setup included primary optics like a Soller slit and anti-scattering screen, and secondary optics with a nickel filter. The purpose of this analysis is to determine the arrangement of the molecules within the hydrogels, distinguishing between crystalline and amorphous regions, and to assess how the incorporation of HA and curcumin affects the structural properties of SF. This information is crucial for understanding the hydrogels' physical characteristics and their potential for biomedical applications, as it relates to drug release and cell interaction.
509e71dde3fb_9b8070eabf4c: This section details the *in vitro* cell response experiments conducted to assess the biocompatibility and bioactivity of silk fibroin/hyaluronic acid (SF/HA) hydrogels, with and without curcumin. The mouse lung fibroblast cell line L929 was cultured in DMEM supplemented with FBS, glutamax, pyruvate, and antibiotics, and incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere. Cytotoxicity was evaluated using the MTT assay, measuring absorbance at 560 nm, with hydrogels sterilized via UV irradiation and incubated with FBS before cell seeding. Cell viability was assessed on days 1, 3, and 7, and cell morphology was observed using a Leica inverted microscope after 72 hours. Statistical analysis, including Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Levene, Tukey’s test, and ANOVA, was performed using GraphPad Prism to determine statistical significance (p < 0.05). This section bridges the material characterization with biological evaluation, setting the stage for the results and discussion on the hydrogels' potential for biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_331329ae0980: This section focuses on the macroscopic characteristics of the synthesized hydrogels, specifically examining the visual appearance of different formulations. The hydrogels are composed of silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), and curcumin, with samples SF, A2, B3, and C4 being visually compared. The key observation is the color variation, particularly the presence of brown coloration in curcumin-containing hydrogels, indicating successful incorporation of the compound. The section also references external research suggesting that HA improves the mechanical properties of hydrogels due to its superhydrophilicity. This section sets the stage for further analysis by providing a preliminary visual assessment of the hydrogels, linking composition to observable properties, and connecting to the broader context of hydrogel mechanical properties, which are crucial for biomedical applications as discussed in the introduction.
509e71dde3fb_5f0020f32131: This section investigates the gelation time of silk fibroin (SF) using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy to analyze structural changes. SF fibers, obtained via degumming, are characterized by typical amide bands (A, B, I, II, III) at specific wavenumbers. The study examines SF samples (3 mg/mL) sonicated for varying durations (1-20 s) to induce gelation, observing a shift in the amide I band. Key findings reveal that increasing sonication time promotes the transition from random coil structures to β-sheets, with at least 5 seconds of sonication required for noticeable β-sheet formation to support gelation. This section details the method for determining the optimal sonication time needed to induce SF gelation, a crucial step in hydrogel preparation for biomedical applications, as described in the broader paper.
509e71dde3fb_2f4f5712856f: This section investigates the chemical structure of composite hydrogels using ATR-FTIR spectroscopy to characterize changes during preparation, focusing on silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), and curcumin. The analysis examines SF/HA hydrogels, SF/curcumin hydrogels, and SF/HA/curcumin hydrogels, prepared after sonication. Key peaks are identified around 1625 cm⁻¹, 1515 cm⁻¹, and 1230 cm⁻¹, corresponding to β-sheet structures. As HA content increases in SF/HA hydrogels, a peak around 1040 cm⁻¹ (alcohol group) significantly increases, indicating HA presence. A key finding is that individual curcumin peaks are not observed in SF/curcumin or SF/HA/curcumin hydrogels due to overlapping vibrational modes, except for a glimpse of a peak at 1140 cm⁻¹ (C-O-C stretching) at the highest curcumin proportions. This section contributes to the paper's objective of characterizing the prepared hydrogels to determine their potential therapeutic effect for biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_af48a2b146c6: This section investigates the cross-sectional morphology of silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), and curcumin hydrogels using Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy (FESEM). The analysis focuses on samples with varying compositions, including SF, SF/HA blends, SF/curcumin combinations, and SF/HA/curcumin composites, with HA concentrations up to 60 wt.% and curcumin concentrations at 5 and 9 wt.%. FESEM images reveal porous scaffold structures with interconnected pores in all samples, with observations noting differences in pore size and homogeneity. The synthesis of sample B1 uses NaOH, influencing pore size. The key finding suggests a synergistic effect between SF, HA, and curcumin, leading to more homogeneous structures in ternary composites. This morphological characterization complements other analyses, contributing to understanding the hydrogels' properties for biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_3be96c2dc9bf: This section analyzes the thermal stability of SF/HA, curcumin-loaded SF, and curcumin-loaded SF/HA hydrogels using thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) and differential thermal analysis (DTA) from room temperature to 800°C. The analysis reveals three main stages of weight loss: initial water evaporation around 120°C, SF degradation above 250°C, and decomposition of residual components above 350°C. Water loss for pure SF ranged from 4.4 to 6.5 wt.%, increasing with HA addition, reaching 14 wt.% in curcumin-loaded SF/HA. DTA curves show a main SF degradation peak between 284-311°C for curcumin-loaded SF, with additional peaks indicating HA and curcumin decomposition at lower temperatures. The findings suggest that the addition of curcumin and HA affects the thermal stability of the SF hydrogel, providing insights into the thermal behavior of these composite biomaterials. This section contributes to the overall characterization of the hydrogels, assessing their suitability for biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_669577df3700: This section analyzes the crystal structure of silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), curcumin, and their composite hydrogels using X-ray diffraction (XRD). The hydrogels examined include SF/HA, curcumin-loaded SF, and curcumin-loaded SF/HA. The XRD patterns were deconvoluted to identify peaks corresponding to silk I and silk II structures. Key findings indicate that the complexation of SF and HA reduces the overall crystallinity of the hydrogel. Furthermore, the addition of curcumin leads to its transition from a crystalline to an amorphous state within the SF and SF/HA matrices, suggesting effective loading and improved solubility. These structural changes, confirmed by d-spacing values, are crucial for enhancing the hydrogels' properties for biomedical applications, aligning with the paper's objective to develop therapeutic biomaterials.
509e71dde3fb_93d2545964dc: This section examines the swelling properties and *in vitro* curcumin release kinetics from silk fibroin (SF) and hyaluronic acid (HA) hydrogels. Swelling tests revealed that SF/HA hydrogels with a 40/60 ratio (C3, C6) exhibited the best water content. Release studies, performed under sink conditions using PBS (pH 7 with 0.5% Tween 80), demonstrated that hydrogels delayed curcumin release compared to free curcumin powder, which reached a plateau at 0.2 hours, while hydrogels containing HA (C4, C9) reached it at 0.5 hours. The addition of HA hindered curcumin release, and sustained release profiles suggest potential antibacterial barrier formation against *Staphylococcus aureus*. This section builds upon material preparation and characterization, investigating the hydrogels' suitability for drug delivery, a key aspect of their potential biomedical applications.
509e71dde3fb_92143328e71d: This section evaluates the cell viability of L929 fibroblast cells seeded into silk fibroin/hyaluronic acid (SF/HA) hydrogels, with and without curcumin, over 1, 3, and 7 days using MTT assays. The objective is to determine curcumin's impact on cell development within the SF/HA hydrogel. The study analyzes cell density, measured by MTT absorbance, and compares the effects of SF/HA, curcumin-loaded SF, and curcumin-loaded SF/HA hydrogels, noting statistical significance (p < 0.05 to p < 0.0001) relative to controls. Key findings indicate that while SF/HA hydrogels initially reduce cell viability, cells adapt and proliferate over time. Curcumin loading positively modifies cell behavior within the SF/HA scaffold, enhancing cell proliferation, particularly at higher concentrations, suggesting improved biocompatibility and potential for tissue engineering applications. This section builds upon the material characterization by assessing biological activity, linking material composition to cellular response.
509e71dde3fb_5e79d7706ca7: This section focuses on cell morphology and overall conclusions of the study, examining the growth status of L929 cells cultured with silk fibroin (SF), hyaluronic acid (HA), and curcumin-loaded SF/HA hydrogels. Microscopic observations of cell growth were conducted on samples A1 and A2 (SF/HA) at 3 days and C4 and C7 (curcumin-loaded SF/HA) at 7 days. The study utilized sonication to prepare hydrogels for biomedical applications, characterizing them using FTIR, XRD, TGA, and FESEM to ensure adequate curcumin loading. Cell viability tests demonstrated that curcumin enhances the therapeutic characteristics of SF/HA, suggesting low cytotoxicity and excellent biocompatibility. The study anticipates synergistic effects in vivo, positioning curcumin-loaded SF/HA hydrogels as potential candidates for wound dressings and tissue engineering scaffolds, with future in vivo assays planned.

e21be6349b3b_a36b2931e79f: This section introduces the critical issue of plastic waste, particularly focusing on flexible plastic packaging and the challenges it poses to mechanical recycling due to printing inks. It highlights the significant consumption of plastics, exceeding 400 million Mg globally in 2019, with Europe consuming 50 million Mg annually in 2020, 40% of which is used for packaging. Low-density polyethylene (LDPE) constitutes a major portion at 8.8 million Mg/a, often used as flexible film, while other polymers like HDPE, PET, and PP are also utilized. The section sets the stage for investigating de-inking methods, specifically using surfactants and alkaline washing, to remove printing ink and improve recyclate quality. It emphasizes the need for data linking de-inking efficiency with ink compositions and process parameters like temperature, NaOH concentration, and retention time, which are investigated in this study.
e21be6349b3b_071651dc8957: This section addresses the management of flexible plastic waste, a significant environmental concern. It categorizes waste into post-industrial and post-consumer sources, noting the higher quality of the former but highlighting limitations due to printing ink contamination, which can introduce unknown and potentially genotoxic substances according to European food safety regulations. The section reports that only 17% of post-consumer flexible packaging waste is effectively recycled in Europe. It describes the sorting process using air classification and NIR spectroscopy, focusing on LDPE while acknowledging challenges with multilayer packaging and PP contamination due to similar densities, hindering separation via sink-swim methods. The recycling process involves shredding, density separation, washing with NaOH, drying, and extrusion, but these advanced technologies are not universally implemented. Contamination, including non-polymer elements like printing inks and surfactants, leads to down-cycling into low-value products.
e21be6349b3b_38bc3f10b7a3: This section addresses printing ink as a major source of contamination in plastic recycling, focusing on flexible packaging. It details the composition of printing inks, including pigments, binders (nitrocellulose), additives, and solvents (organic or water/alcohol-based), while noting the irrelevance of evaporated solvents in recycling. The section mentions UV and electron beam curing inks, and the use of corona discharge for adhesion on polyolefins, forming hydroxy, carbonyl, and carboxyl groups. Table 1, referenced at the end, likely presents a typical composition of printing ink. The section fits into the paper's introduction by establishing the problem of ink contamination in plastic recycling and setting the stage for subsequent investigations into de-inking methods.
e21be6349b3b_ec6fe60e510a: This section addresses the problems caused by printing ink in the mechanical recycling of flexible plastic packaging. It highlights that the presence of printing ink leads to discoloration of recyclates, reducing their market value, and lowers their tensile strength. The instability of ink components, particularly nitrocellulose (NC) binder resin, under typical extrusion temperatures (150-240 °C) is discussed, noting its thermal degradation starting at 160-185 °C, which produces undesirable effects like brownish color, porosity, and odor. Specific organic pigments, such as PR 146 and PY 13, are also mentioned as thermally unstable. This section builds upon the introduction by detailing specific contaminants and their effects, setting the stage for subsequent sections that explore de-inking solutions to mitigate these issues.
e21be6349b3b_7d17e3f7bcd5: This section focuses on surfactant cleaning as a method for removing printing ink from flexible plastic packaging, specifically LDPE films, highlighting its potential as a more suitable alternative to mechanical and chemical cleaning due to the hazards and costs associated with organic solvents. The detergency cleaning process involves removing ink ("soil") and suspending it in a cleaning solution ("bath"), with key steps including surfactant adsorption, ink removal, detachment, and stabilization. Soil removal, breaking mechanical and chemical bonds like hydrogen bonds, covalent bonds, and Van der Waals forces, is crucial. Given that de-inking experiments are conducted above the critical micelle concentration (CMC), solubilization of the binder in the micelle is identified as the dominant mechanism. This section sets the stage for evaluating the effectiveness of different surfactants and conditions in subsequent experiments, contributing to the paper's overall aim of optimizing de-inking processes for plastic recycling.
e21be6349b3b_eb86eee8ffb0: This section presents a literature review of previous de-inking studies, focusing on the effectiveness of various surfactants in removing inks from plastic films composed of 70% LDPE and 30% HDPE. The studies examined water-based inks with different colors and employed surfactants such as Sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), Cetrimonium bromide (CTAB), Hexadecylpyridinium chloride (CPC), Nonylphenol polyethoxylated (NP(EO)10), Dimethyl “DAO. oxide, Ethoxylated alcohol, and Ethoxylated amine (AMEOS5). The results indicate that de-inking is partially effective above the CMC concentration for anionic surfactants at pH 8-9, while cationic surfactants are effective above the CMC at pH 5-12. Nonionic surfactants achieve almost complete de-inking at pH 10-12 above the CMC. Amphoteric surfactants show effective de-inking across a broad pH range (5-12) above the CMC. This section provides background information for the current study, highlighting the importance of surfactant type, concentration, and pH in the de-inking process.
e21be6349b3b_42395d6a8fdb: This section presents a compilation of previous de-inking studies, focusing on the effectiveness of various surfactants on different plastic films printed with solvent-based inks. Key entities include LDPE, HDPE, HDPE bottles, solvent-based inks with epoxy resin, PET-derived de-inking agents, and waste cooking oil-derived surfactants. The studies explore various surfactants like SDS, SDO$s, polyalkylene oxide modified polydimethylsiloxanes, dimethyl dodecylamine oxide (DDAO), ethoxylated amine (AMEOS), CTAB, DTAB, TTAB, GD-pyr-Br, CT-pyr-Br, W111+DA850, and biosurfactants. The results indicate varying de-inking effects depending on the surfactant category (anionic, nonionic, amphoteric, cationic), pH levels (ranging from 1 to 13), temperatures (30°C to 50°C), retention times (15 minutes to 2 hours), and surfactant concentrations (5% and CMC multiples). Notably, cationic surfactants often demonstrate complete de-inking under specific alkaline conditions, while some nonionic surfactants show promising results. This section provides a background on existing de-inking methods, setting the stage for the current study's investigation into the de-inkability of different printing ink compositions.
e21be6349b3b_6c3083385e00: This section introduces the research gap concerning the de-inkability of plastic packaging printing inks, focusing on the influence of ink components like binders, pigments, and over-printing varnish under varying conditions of temperature, pH, surfactant type, and retention time. It highlights the limitations of previous studies that categorized inks solely by carrier type (solvent-based vs. water-based) and lacked detailed pigment information. The current study aims to evaluate the de-inkability of common printing inks using existing surfactants, provide an open-source evaluation method, and derive process parameters for integrating de-inking into recycling plants. The section then transitions into the materials and methods, describing the tested samples as films with common surface printing ink systems, including nitrocellulose (NC), pigment red (PR), pigment yellow (PY), pigment black (PBk), pigment blue (PB), cellulose acetate propionate (CAP), and polyurethane (PU) based inks, provided by Siegwerk Druckfarben AG & Co.KGaA. e21be6349b3b_24aeaa8c08c8: This section outlines the materials used in the de-inking experiments, specifically detailing the composition of various plastic film samples with different printing ink systems. e21be6349b3b_95fd105e5506: This section outlines the experimental design for evaluating the de-inkability of printing inks on plastic packaging, focusing on the impact of different ink components and cleaning agents. e21be6349b3b_41badf173989: This section outlines the experimental design for evaluating the cleaning performance of various detergents on printed plastic films. It details four distinct test conditions (A, B, C, and D) simulating different scenarios in recycling plants, ranging from "cold washing" without NaOH to "hot-washing" with varying NaOH concentrations. Condition A mimics current recycling practices at 40°C, while Condition C represents hot washing. Condition B is an intermediate setting to explore energy reduction potential, and Condition D is reserved for samples resistant to de-inking under milder conditions. The section references Table 5, which provides a concise overview of these testing conditions, including NaOH concentration, temperature, surfactant concentration, and retention time, setting the stage for subsequent analysis of de-inking efficiency.
e21be6349b3b_a7fcc1d30f4d: This section outlines the experimental conditions used to assess the de-inkability of various printing inks on plastic packaging. It details four distinct washing scenarios (A, B, C, and D) with varying concentrations of sodium hydroxide (NaOH), temperatures, surfactant concentrations, and retention times. Condition A simulates current recycling plants without NaOH addition, using a temperature of 40°C and 0.25 wt.% surfactant for 15 minutes. Conditions B and C represent "middle point" and "hot-washing" scenarios, respectively, with increased NaOH concentrations (1 wt.% and 2 wt.%) and temperatures (55°C and 70°C), while maintaining the same surfactant concentration and retention time. Condition D is reserved for samples that showed no de-inking under A-C, employing a high NaOH concentration (5 wt.%), elevated temperature (80°C), and extended retention time (60 minutes). e21be6349b3b_01cdfca301c2: This section details the experimental procedure used to assess the de-inking efficiency of various surfactants on printed plastic films. The process begins with preparing solutions containing surfactants (0.5 g), NaOH (0.2-1.0 g, depending on the test condition), and water to a total weight of 200 g in a beaker. Sample flakes are added, and the mixture is agitated at 800 rpm on a heating plate. Color change is measured using a colorimeter, and after a set retention time, the flakes are separated, and the liquid phase is collected for flocculation. The experimental procedure and equipment are visually summarized in Figure 1. This section is crucial for understanding the methodology used to generate the results presented later in the paper, specifically regarding the de-inking rates achieved under different conditions.
e21be6349b3b_e4d2f47c7a30: This section details the method used to quantitatively evaluate the effectiveness of the de-inking process on plastic films. The de-inking performance is assessed by measuring the color difference, represented as L-a-b values according to the CIELAB standard, before and after treatment. Nine randomly selected flakes from each sample are glued to white paper, scanned, and analyzed using a custom Python 3.10 program (code in Supplementary Material S2). The color change is then calculated using equations (1) and (2) to determine the de-inking rate (DI), where 100 signifies complete de-inking and 0 indicates no de-inking. The variables in the de-inking rate equation include the sample number (from Table 3), detergent used (I-VI from Table 4), and the experimental condition (A-D from Table 5). This method provides a standardized, open-source approach for quantifying de-inkability, linking visual changes to numerical values for comparison across different ink compositions and washing scenarios.
e21be6349b3b_98a7241600fc: This section focuses on evaluating the detergents used in the de-inking experiments by calculating their hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) values using Davies' method. The HLB value is determined using Equation (3), which incorporates the values of hydrophilic and hydrophobic functional groups present in the detergents. The variables in the equation are defined as: *Hj* representing the value of the hydrophilic groups, *m* representing the number of hydrophilic groups, *o* representing the hydrophilic groups, and *n* representing the number of hydrophobic groups. The HLB values of the functional groups are obtained from cited references. This evaluation aims to correlate the detergents' HLB values with their de-inking performance, providing insights into the optimal balance of hydrophilic and lipophilic properties for effective ink removal from plastic packaging, which is a key component of the overall study.
e21be6349b3b_9a954fa5a005: This section bridges the experimental methods and the presentation of results, focusing on water treatment and the study's outcomes. It begins by detailing the water treatment process following de-inking, involving stirring the liquid phase at 150 rpm with 1 v/v% flocculation agent (SEPAR Chemie AW+KW), followed by vacuum filtration using 15-micrometer porosity filter paper (Rotilabo Type 601A), and photometric analysis from 900 to 300 nm. The section then outlines the structure of the results, dividing them into three parts: the influence of printing ink components on de-inkability, the performance of different cleaning agents, and the efficiency of flocculation after de-inking. A 95% de-inking rate is defined as complete de-inking based on visual observations. The section emphasizes the importance of flocculation for water reusability in recycling plants, setting the stage for the subsequent presentation and analysis of the experimental findings.
e21be6349b3b_7dfb22671aab: This section investigates the influence of different pigments on the de-inking process of plastic packaging, focusing on Samples 1-5 where pigment type is the sole variable. The study examines pigments PR 57:1, PR 146, PY 13, PBk 7 (carbon black), and PB 15:4, evaluating their de-inking performance under various detergent and condition combinations, referencing experimental results presented in Figure 2. e21be6349b3b_1ae0d6f77708: This section investigates the influence of different binder types (NC, PU, PVB, and UV-crosslinked acrylate) without overprint varnish (OPV) on de-inking behavior, observing solubilization for NC/PU and peeling for PVB/UV-acrylate. e21be6349b3b_0cab274752b4: This section examines the impact of crosslinked overprint varnishes (OPV) on the de-inkability of nitrocellulose (NC) binder systems, comparing samples with varying degrees of crosslinking. e21be6349b3b_795381ff83af: This section investigates the de-inking challenges of polyurethane (PU) binders when combined with crosslinked polyvinyl butyral (PVB) overprint varnishes (OPV), a common requirement for commercial applications. e21be6349b3b_88a7a2aa1a48: This section evaluates the performance of six different detergents (I-VI) under varying conditions (A-D) for de-inking different plastic packaging materials, as illustrated in Figure 8. e21be6349b3b_a5e0ca315842: This section analyzes the de-inking performance of various detergents under different conditions, focusing on the impact of crosslinked structures and hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB). ecaf42a5e4ac_cefc65379a1d: This section introduces the research on H+-conducting aromatic multiblock copolymers and blend membranes for PEM electrolysis, positioning green hydrogen production via water electrolysis as a key energy storage solution. ecaf42a5e4ac_e5b9192b060c: This section details the two-step synthesis of multiblock-co-ionomers (MBIs) for proton exchange membranes. ecaf42a5e4ac_319b47ae6251: This section details the preparation of three-component blend ionomer membranes (7CBM) using specific polymers: an aromatic polyether synthesized from bisphenol AF and decafluorobiphenyl, pyridine-modified polyethersulfone (PSU-Py), and partially fluorinated polybenzimidazole (F¢-PBI). The synthesis of the aromatic polyether involves sulfonation with H2SO4 containing 30% free SO3. PSU-Py is prepared via lithiation of PSU Udel followed by reaction with isonicotinic acid methyl ester. The section highlights the advantages of using polybenzimidazole for improved stability and PSU-Py for loose ionic cross-links, contributing to proton conduction. The blend membranes are prepared by dissolving the sulfonated polymer (2.55 g) in N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) to create a 20 wt% solution, neutralizing with triethylamine, and then adding F¢-PBI (0.15 g) and PSU-Py (0.3 g) dissolved in DMAc (5 wt%/10 wt%). ecaf42a5e4ac_2c200c13b9e0: This section details the methods used to characterize the synthesized polymers and membranes, focusing on their water uptake and ion-exchange capacity (IEC). The characterization aims to quantify key properties relevant to proton conductivity and performance in PEM electrolysis. Water uptake (WU) is determined by measuring the wet and dry weights of the membranes, and the hydration number (λ) is calculated to quantify water molecules per SO3H group. IEC, a measure of the sulfonic acid groups' concentration, is determined through acid-base titration using NaOH and HCl solutions with a concentration of 0.1 N. Equations are provided for calculating WU, λ, IECdirect, and IECtotal, using parameters like membrane mass and titrant volumes. These characterization techniques provide essential data for understanding the structure-property relationships of the synthesized materials and their suitability for PEM electrolysis applications, building upon the polymer synthesis described earlier in the paper.
ecaf42a5e4ac_9dfba6f173be: This section details the experimental methods used to characterize the synthesized polymers and membranes, focusing on electrochemical and thermal properties. Electrochemical Impedance Spectroscopy (EIS) was employed using two different setups: a Zahner Elektrik workstation for conductivity measurements in 0.5 N H2SO4 solution at room temperature, and a Scribner Associates Membrane Test System for in-situ measurements between 30 and 110 °C at 90% relative humidity, utilizing gas diffusion layers and platinum electrodes. Thermal stability was assessed via Thermogravimetric Analysis (TGA) coupled with Fourier-Transform Infrared Spectroscopy (FTIR), heating samples in an oxygen-rich atmosphere (60-75% O2) at 20 K/min up to 600 °C. This allowed for identification of SO3H group splitting-off (Tso3H-onset) and backbone degradation (Tco-onset) by monitoring S=O and C=O vibrations, respectively. These techniques provide crucial data for evaluating the potential of the synthesized materials for PEM electrolysis applications.
ecaf42a5e4ac_57d15e1ab257: This section details the size exclusion chromatography (SEC) or gel permeation chromatography (GPC) method used to determine the molecular weight distribution (MWD) of synthesized polymers. The technique fractionates polymers based on hydrodynamic volume, yielding number-average molecular weight (Mn) and weight-average molecular weight (Mw), where Mn is less than Mw. Polydispersity (PD), calculated as Mw/Mn, indicates the MWD width. Calibration was performed using a polystyrene standard (PSS ReadyCal Kit). N,N-dimethylacetamide (DMAc) with 5.0 g/L lithium bromide (LiBr) served as the mobile phase. An Agilent Technologies 1200 Series GPC system with differential refractometer, viscometer, and multi-angle light scattering (MALLS) photometer detectors was employed. Separation columns from Polymer Standards Service GmbH (PSS) with varying pore sizes (PSS PFG, 5-7 um, 300 A; PSS PFG 5-7 um, 1000 A) constituted the stationary phase. This method is crucial for characterizing the synthesized polymers, providing essential data for correlating polymer structure with membrane properties and performance in PEM electrolysis, as discussed throughout the paper.
ecaf42a5e4ac_b5794c2cee78: This section details the method used to determine the hydrogen permeability of synthesized and reference membranes, a crucial factor for water electrolyzer safety and efficiency. The technique employed was improved linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) with varying sweep rates (2-10 mV/s) to extrapolate current free of capacitive effects. The setup involved electrolysis cells from balticFuelCells within a Greenlight E100 test station, using a ModuLab XM ECS for LSV measurements. Electrodes were prepared by spray coating an ink containing 20 wt% Nafion D520 and 80% platinum on carbon catalyst in a 1:4 2-propanol/water mixture onto H4Cs gas diffusion layers, achieving a Pt loading of 0.2 mg/cm². The method assumes diffusive hydrogen transport through the aqueous membrane phase, described by Fick's first law, allowing calculation of the hydrogen permeability coefficient (Kp, H2). This section provides the experimental basis for comparing the hydrogen crossover performance of the synthesized multiblock-co-ionomers and blend membranes against commercial Nafion membranes, linking membrane properties to electrolyzer performance.
ecaf42a5e4ac_e4ee10248495: This section details the fabrication process of Membrane Electrode Assemblies (MEAs) used for water electrolysis testing. Nafion 212 membranes were pre-soaked in deionized water for 30 minutes, whereas Multiblock-co-Ionomer and blend membranes were used as synthesized. MEA compression was achieved using PTFE gaskets with thicknesses of 0.18 mm and 1.00 mm at the cathode and anode, respectively, resulting in approximately 28% compression. This section provides the necessary experimental details for replicating the MEA construction, a crucial step for evaluating the performance of the synthesized membranes in water electrolysis.
ecaf42a5e4ac_606015b3aa39: This section details the experimental setup for electrolysis tests and presents the preparation and characterization of ionomers and ionomer blend membranes. ecaf42a5e4ac_678e75638826: This section investigates the discrepancy between theoretical and experimental chain lengths of hydrophilic and hydrophobic blocks used in multiblock-co-ionomer synthesis. It focuses on the observation that hydrophilic chains are shorter than predicted, unlike hydrophobic chains. The proposed explanation involves a side reaction during hydrophilic block polycondensation where the K₂CO₃ catalyst causes hydrolytic splitting of F ions from fluorinated oligomer end groups, terminating chain growth. To validate this, a hydrolytic stability test was performed on SDFDPS, DFDPS, and Decafluorobiphenyl using a 12-fold excess of K₂CO₃ in NMP at 130 °C for 24 hours, with 1H NMR used to analyze the products. The key finding is that hydrolytic cleavage of F ions occurs only in SDFDPS, confirming the proposed side reaction due to the electron-withdrawing effect of the sulfonate group. This section elucidates a critical synthetic challenge and its underlying mechanism, contributing to a better understanding of multiblock-co-ionomer synthesis, a key aspect of the overall paper.
ecaf42a5e4ac_03a5138d6439: This section details the synthesis and characterization of multiblock-co-ionomers (MBIs) formed by coupling hydrophilic (PKK) and hydrophobic (PFS) blocks via polycondensation at an equimolar ratio. ecaf42a5e4ac_376a36cf0a02: This section investigates the electrochemical properties of three membranes – 3C-BM, MBI-MS, and Nafion 212 – using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) at temperatures ranging from 30 to 110 °C with 90% humidification using a Scribner device.
